Mama Cash partner pushed forward their mission to protect and strengthen WHRDs’ activism by influencing a proposed 2020 Human Rights Defenders Protection Bill to include provisions that address the specific struggles and needs of their community. They did so by pro-actively advocating with policy makers in Uganda. For instance, they held a meeting with the Uganda Women Parliamentary Association and members of parliament. The network also presented a position paper on the topic. In response, key legal officials publicly committed to incorporating the needs and demands of WHRDs into the bill. For example, a senior legislator committed to incorporating a gender lens when revising working definitions of discrimination and victimization based on recommendations presented by the Network in their position paper. In 2020, ELWOFOD worked in coordination with the Women Against Women Custodial Justices Movement (WAWCI), a network of 10 feminist, advocacy organizations, to petition the Uasin-Gishu County Assembly to acknowledge and address the needs of ex-prisoners, women sex workers, girls, trans people and intersex people in the county’s Integrated Development Plan and Fiscal Budget. As part of this effort, ELWOFOD advocated the County to address the discrimination faced by women ex-prisoners in accessing the Affirmative Action Fund. This Fund, which falls under the Ministry of Public Service, Youth and Gender Affairs, was enacted through the Public Finance Management Act, 2012 as part of the Government’s commitment to redress past, economic disadvantages among certain segments of the population, including women, youth and persons with disabilities. ELWOFOD and WAWCI concerted efforts with the County Government resulted in increased funding to vulnerable women. 10% of the County’s budget was allocated to women’s groups through the Affirmative Action Fund, representing a 5% increase compared to previous years. Furthermore, ELWOFOD was given the opportunity to manage the Langas County Market. Through this opportunity, 20 women ex-prisoners take home 40% of the revenues earned daily. Another 12 ex-prisoners have also become employed through the nation-wide National Hygiene Programme (Kazi Mtaani), which provides members of vulnerable populations in Kenya who live in informal settlements to undertake projects that improve urban infrastructure and sustain public goods. These combined wins have provided more financial security to members of ELWOFOD’s community while also potentially setting precedents for how funding is disbursed to women ex-prisoners. Groups in many countries in Africa are working under very restrictive and violent laws against LBTQI rights. Most groups did not report on improving, changing, or blocking any laws and/or policies in 2023. However, their advocacy work is targeted at local government officials (MPs) and national committees and is ongoing. One group in Senegal improved their constituencies, which mainly includes sex workers, access to local health care services through their advocacy work.

The reporting indicator is unique, considering it takes a long time to influence laws, policies and strategies used at the national level. This will be a 5-year target. The achievement of laws and policies will be counted only once.

National and local government and economic spaces for accesses resourcing and strengthening the implementation of laws and policies. Groups in Africa participated in national, regional, and Global events. Through alliances and coalitions, they presented sessions during CSW in NYC and worked to influence cross-country projects that were led by the World Bank, for example. Defending spaces also meant participating in national human rights commissions, as was the case for one group based in Uganda that works within movements to advocate for building an intersectional, feminist lens when advocating for human rights. Thus same group also engages in different human rights networks and commissions in Uganda and across the region, as well as through the CEDAW committee, which protects the rights and duties of human rights defenders.
